pageData.title: The Chimú Empire
pageData.para1: The Chimu Empire. The Chimu were the largest and most prosperous culture of the Late Intermediate Period along the Peruvian coast, flourishing between the 12th and 15th centuries CE with their capital at the great city of Chan Chan. The Chimu constructed cities and developed large-scale irrigation systems using canals, and there seems to have been much social stratification. Rulers like Guacricaur expanded into the Moche, Santa, and Zana valleys, and in 1375 CE, under Nancinpinco, the Chimu conquered the Lambayeque (Sican) culture, absorbing some of its cultural practices; tribute extracted through successful military campaigns and political coercion made them the dominant regional power, with Chan Chan the capital of administrative centers across the valleys. This empire matters because it was the last great coastal civilization before the Inca, and its methods - in administration, craft, and imperial organization - were studied by its conquerors.
pageData.para2: The Chimu spoke the Yunca language - also called Mochica or Moche - now extinct and definitely distinct from the Inca tongue, and they produced characteristic black ware ceramics. Their imperial system was sophisticated: conquered rulers were allowed a certain autonomy, and compounds of foreign artisans were gathered in the capital, a policy the Inca would later adopt. The empire's independence ended when the Inca, under Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui and his son Topa Inca Yupanqui, conquered it between 1465 and 1470 CE, capturing the 11th known Chimu ruler, Minchancaman, around 1470; thereafter the Chimu became a vassal state within the Inca Empire. Yet the story does not end there - the imperial playbook the Inca inherited, from road-fed tribute to artisan compounds, carried the imprint of the coastal kingdom it had absorbed.

pageData.title: The Inca Empire (Tahuantinsuyu)
pageData.para1: The Inca Empire: Tahuantinsuyu. The Inca Empire, known to its people as Tahuantinsuyu - 'The Four Parts Together' - arose sometime in the early 1400s and became the largest indigenous empire of the Americas. How much of that growth owes to a single great leader, an Alexander-the-Great-like Pachacuti? Scholars note the Incas had been developing the capability for conquest over four to six generations, though the 1586 chronicle of the Spanish cleric Miguel Cabello Valboa dates Pachacuti's reign to 1438-1471 and his son Tupac Inca Yupanqui's to the years that followed. The empire matters because it bound the Andes into a single administered world, from imperial Cuzco outward, through a system of administration and infrastructure unmatched anywhere in the pre-Columbian Americas.
pageData.para2: At the heart of that system was a vast network of roads - some 40,000 kilometers according to John Hyslop, the leading scholar of the subject - built to move armies and administrative resources across a hugely varied landscape, connecting the capital to provincial centers, with many smaller branches extending to outposts east and west; the roads varied in width and style because Inca leaders often utilized existing routes. Around Cuzco, workers received their food from state storehouses every four days or even daily, and below the emperor, religious officials and magistrates called kurakas oversaw the day-to-day administration of their regions, collecting taxes, overseeing day-to-day administration, and even choosing brides for the men of their communities. The empire's end came swiftly: after a devastating civil war between the half-brothers Atahualpa and Huascar, the Spaniard Pizarro captured and executed Atahualpa, dealing a fatal blow to what had been the largest indigenous empire of the Americas.

pageData.title: The Muisca Confederation
pageData.para1: The Muisca Confederation. The Muisca civilization flourished in the fertile eastern highlands of what is now Colombia between 600 and 1600 CE, its territory encompassing modern Bogota and its environs, and it has gained lasting fame as the origin of the legend of El Dorado - 'The Gilded One'. A Muisca ceremony held at Lake Guatavita - actually only one of many kinds - involved a ruler being covered in gold dust; the Spanish, hearing this story, allowed their imagination and lust for gold to leap beyond the bounds of reality, and soon a legend arose of a magnificent golden kingdom. This confederation matters because its goldwork is among the great artistic traditions of the Americas: for the Muisca, gold was not used as a currency but as an artistic medium, mined from exposed veins and panned from mountain rivers.
pageData.para2: The Muisca goldsmiths employed a wide range of techniques - lost-wax casting, a two-tone finish, repousse, soldering, granulation, and filigree - and hammered gold into thin sheets on round stone anvils. Their tunjos - small votive figures of snakes and flat male, female, and animal forms in gold alloy - were placed at sacred sites, and elite members of society wore pectorals, earrings, and nose studs. Nor did they restrict their art to gold: they created fine textiles of wool or cotton. There is ample evidence that commodities such as gold, shells, feathers, animal skins, tobacco, salt, and coca leaves moved through Muisca markets in a thriving regional trade. When the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, drawn by the very legend the Muisca had inspired, this rich highland world was drawn into the colonial age.

pageData.title: The Aymara Kingdoms
pageData.para1: The Aymara Kingdoms. The Aymara kingdoms - also called the lake kingdoms - developed between 1150 and 1477 CE in the high plateau around Lake Titicaca, in the region Andeans called Qullaw, after the disappearance of Tiwanaku left a political vacuum. In its wake, a number of Aymara-speaking, independent, and rival kingdoms emerged, among them the Lupaca, the Colla, the Pacajes, and the Azangaros. Their world was divided between Urcosuyu - 'male, fire' - on the western side of the lake and Umasuyu - 'female, water' - on the eastern side, and their societies often had two leaders apiece; most of these kingdoms buried their leaders in tower-shaped mausoleums, and each held lands at different altitudes in what scholars call a 'vertical archipelago'. These kingdoms matter because they kept the Andean altiplano's ancient ways alive through the centuries between empires, and their lords would play decisive roles in the fate of the Inca.
pageData.para2: The kingdoms warred constantly - above all the rivalry between the Aymara kurakas of Chucuito, of the Lupaca kingdom, and Hatunqulla, of the Colla kingdom. When the Inca pressed south, the Lupaca leader Cari faced the Colla leader Chuqui Capac, who attacked the Lupacas near Paucarcolla before the Inca army arrived; after a long battle near Hatunqulla, Chuqui Capac was taken prisoner, and the Colla lands were subdued - some by force, others peacefully. Destroyed towns were repopulated with mitmakunas, resettled colonists, and the Aymara kingdoms accepted the dominion of Cuzco while keeping their lands and their far-off colonies in the eastern mountains. That arrangement survived until the first years of the Spanish conquest, when the kingdoms' territorial and political dismemberment began.
